tagline.text: A migratory-bird haven and vast floodplain wetland close to Manila

location.label: Location
location.text: Candaba, Pampanga (Doña Simang and Vizal San Pablo area)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (day trip from Manila, transport included)

children.text: Candaba Swamp is a large wetland on the Pampanga plain, about 60km north of Manila, where migratory birds from the Siberia and China side gather in winter. It makes a good day trip for early-morning birdwatching and a walk along the dikes between rice fields.
Candaba Swamp is a low-lying wetland about
60km
north of Manila, spread across Candaba in Pampanga and the surrounding towns. Wikipedia and other sources describe ponds, swamps, marshes and seasonally flooded grassland together as roughly
32,000 hectares

. Every rainy season the whole swamp goes under water, and from about November to April the water recedes and the land becomes farmland planted with crops such as watermelon and rice. The same place therefore looks completely different depending on the season.

Birds are what put this place on travelers' maps. According to reports citing the DENR Biodiversity Management Bureau, about 54 resident species and about 68 migratory species have been recorded here since 1940. They include globally threatened birds such as the Philippine duck, Baer's pochard and streaked reed warbler. The swamp is one of the Philippines' Important Bird Areas (IBA), and many sources describe its Ramsar listing as a candidacy still in progress. Please check official announcements for the current listing status.
Inside the swamp lies the Candaba Swamp Wildlife Reserve. It covers about
72 hectares

and was protected on private initiative, and in 2004 a local ordinance declared the whole municipality of Candaba a bird sanctuary and banned hunting and poaching of wild birds. Some descriptions mention an observation deck and a dike walking trail about
4km
long. Facilities may change from year to year, however.

The atmosphere is closer to a nature outing, looking for birds among rice fields and ponds, than to a manicured park. There are no flashy attractions, but you can make a round trip from Manila in a day, and it is very rewarding if you love birds and photography. On the other hand there are almost no amenities, and at some times of year you cannot get in at all, so timing and preparation matter.
You are said to see the most birds between November and February. Great egrets, common moorhens, black-winged stilts, purple swamphens, garganey and Philippine ducks appear in local birding records.
Bird activity is said to peak between
and
. If you set out before sunrise and arrive then, the sun is gentle and the birds come closer.
Descriptions say the roughly 72-hectare reserve has an observation deck and hides for watching birds unseen. Whether it is open now needs to be confirmed.
You walk unpaved dike paths and watch the birds among the paddies. The terrain is flat, so it is easy on the legs. After rain the paths turn muddy.
In the dry season watermelon and rice grow on the drained land. Candaba is also known for its melons, and the swamp soil is said to be fertile and rich in humus.
Local guides and news reports mention experiences such as wetland walks, fishing, carabao cart rides and local meals. Please ask in advance whether they are currently offered.

Small rivers such as the Maasim, San Miguel, Garlang, Bulu and Peñaranda drain into it. In the rainy season it holds the water and releases it into the Pampanga River, acting as a natural retention basin.

The Ibon-Ebon Festival, whose name means "birds and eggs," was held on February 1–2 in 2008. Some years events are held around World Wetlands Day on February 2, so check the schedule with the Candaba tourist information center.
Set out from Manila. If you have no car, it is easier for dawn birding to stay the night before in Pampanga or in Baliwag, Bulacan.
Arrive in Candaba, sign in at the information point on the reserve side and pay the entrance fee. Past reports mention around
, but you need to confirm this locally.
Walk slowly along the dikes and pond edges looking for birds. Keep your voice low and it is better to stay in one spot for a while.
As the sun gets stronger the birds thin out. Sort your photos and notes and head back.
Move to Candaba or San Fernando town for lunch. Many reports say there are no restaurants inside the swamp.
Bring water and snacks yourself without fail. Buy them at a market or convenience store before you arrive.

items.title: Pampanga combined course
items.subtitle: Candaba with San Fernando and Arayat

children.text: Finish early-morning birding at Candaba Swamp.
Drive toward San Fernando and look around the town's church and market.
Have lunch with Kapampangan local food. Some shops near the swamp sell buro (fermented rice and fish) and salted duck eggs.
If time remains, head toward Mount Arayat to enjoy the scenery, then return to Manila.

items.title: From Manila by car or rental car

children.text: From Manila take NLEX toward the San Fernando exit, continue onto JASA (Gapan–Olongapo Road), and head toward Santa Ana and Candaba.
The Candaba Viaduct carrying NLEX crosses over the swamp, so you can get a sense of its scale from nearby.
The destination is the reserve in the Doña Simang or Vizal San Pablo area. Map-app coordinates may differ slightly, so confirm with the information office by phone.

One description says it is about 5 minutes by private vehicle from the town proper to the reserve, but bringing vehicles deep into the wetland startles the birds, so it is better to park at the entrance and walk.
Some travelers report taking a bus from a northern Manila terminal to Baliwag, Bulacan (for example Baliwag Transit), getting off in Baliwag and continuing to Candaba by tricycle.
Another option described is taking a bus to San Fernando and then a jeepney to Candaba from near the mall in San Fernando. Service intervals are irregular, so move early in the morning.
One report says visitors had to walk from where the paved road ends at Doña Simang to the reserve, which is about
3km
, or
40 minutes
on foot.
Routes and fares change. Check recent information with the Candaba tourist information center (the number in one report is +63 45 632 1299) or the local government.
From Clark International Airport (CRK) you travel to Candaba on roads inside Pampanga. A rental car or ride-hailing service is convenient.
When coming up from Manila (NAIA), the usual approach is to leave the airport toward NLEX and head north.
Within Candaba town, tricycles run between villages. Past reports record a tricycle to the reserve costing at least
one way.
Mobile signal is reported to be weak on the walking approach, so download an offline map.

For birding, the best time is said to be from November, when the migratory birds arrive, to February or March of the following year. Activity peaks from dawn to early morning and in the late afternoon before sunset. In the Philippines, birds tend to gather in one place as the water drains with the start of the dry season.

Around September and October in the rainy season, notices say the swamp floods and it becomes hard to enter the reserve. When typhoons pass, the Pampanga River can overflow and cause sudden floods, so check the weather forecast when planning.

Many reports say there are almost no commercial facilities inside the swamp. Past records mention lodging on the reserve side, but it has not been confirmed whether it operates now. Most visitors stay in San Fernando or Baliwag and travel in early in the morning. A farm-style resort near Candaba town has also been mentioned.

Take care of food in town. Candaba is known for fish caught in the swamp and for duck eggs, and buro (fermented rice and fish) and salted duck eggs are described as local foods. Hunting is banned and there is a history of avian influenza outbreaks, so wild-bird dishes are not recommended, and even if someone sells them it is better not to eat them.

For a day trip it is convenient to eat and shop in San Fernando or Baliwag before heading into Candaba. Candaba is said to be famous for its melons, so in season you may taste them at the market. When returning to Manila, leave early to avoid the NLEX rush-hour traffic.
Arrive between
and
in the early morning to see the most birds.
Binoculars are essential, and many reports say you need a telephoto lens of at least 300mm for photos.
Wear shoes that can get muddy, and bring a hat and sunscreen.
Bring your own water, snacks and a bag for trash. There are no shops in the swamp.
Move quietly so the birds are not startled, and never make loud noises such as gunshots.
Do not take cars and motorcycles deep into the reserve; park at the entrance and walk.
Before you go, phone the Candaba tourist information center or the local government to confirm admission, fees and guide bookings.
Starting from Manila, an early dawn departure is easier; allow for NLEX congestion on holidays.
If you are new to birding, joining a Wild Bird Club of the Philippines event or going with a local guide makes it easier to identify birds.
In the rainy season (roughly September–October) the swamp floods and access to the reserve can be blocked, so be sure to confirm it is open before you set out.
Entrance fees, guide fees and contact numbers come from old reports, so they need to be confirmed locally.

Some assessments say the habitat has shrunk greatly compared with the past, and conversion to rice fields, poaching and water hyacinth growth are cited as threats. Do not chase birds or flush them for photos.
There is almost no shade and a risk of heatstroke at midday. Do not walk for long at midday.
Mobile signal is weak in some stretches and the paths branch, so prepare an offline map.
Some residents have suffered long-term flooding, so be considerate when you talk about floods and displacement.

A mountain rising in the middle of the Pampanga plain north of the swamp. It is in the same area as Candaba, so it pairs well in one day. Travel time depends on local road conditions, so check in advance.
As the capital of Pampanga it has many restaurants, markets and places to stay, making it a base before and after a Candaba visit.
A city in Bulacan that serves as the stop where you get on and off the bus toward Candaba, with churches and crafts.
The airport and urban area in Pampanga, and the starting point when you arrive by plane.
